# Introduction

As documented [here](https://communities.sas.com/t5/SASware-Ballot-Ideas/Confidence-limits-using-the-Miettinen-Nurminen-stratified-method/idi-p/829317), there is a requirement to use methods other than the simple Approximate Normal (Wald) method, for confidence intervals (CIs) for comparing proportions from stratified datasets. In certain cases, for example, when you have a baseline imbalance of stratification factors, or when the treatment allocation scheme was stratified, it is important to control for the stratification factors. Stratified analysis may also be employed when combining the results of two pivotal trials for an Integrated Summary of Efficacy (although the validity of such a meta-analysis using only two studies may be questionable).

The stratified Miettinen-Nurminen 1985 asymptotic score method is of particular interest, because it is often recommended and used by regulatory authorities for clinical trial submissions. It is particularly relevant for non-inferiority trials, where the confidence limits correspond to hypothesis tests with the variance estimated under the (non-zero) null hypothesis. A modification of the stratified score approach is provided by the Skewness-Corrected Asymptotic Score (SCAS) method, for potential improvement in type 1 error rates achieved by such one-sided tests, especially for ratio contrasts or designs with uneven treatment allocation.

Note that Miettinen & Nurminen defined methods for estimating relative risk (RR) and odds ratio (OR), as well as for the risk difference (RD). Also note that there are variations of the Miettinen-Nurminen method, depending on the weights used: the original version as published in the 1985 paper uses an iterative weighting scheme. An alternative simpler version using Mantel-Haenszel weighting is often employed instead for RD, having been found to produce similar results in a 2008 ASA paper[@lu2008].

`SAS PROC FREQ` in Base SAS (up to v9.4) does not produce a stratified MN confidence interval. The default output includes CIs using the Mantel-Haenszel (Approximate Normal) and Summary Score methods. Stratified MN CIs for RD have more recently been added to `PROC FREQ` within the SAS Viya platform. The only other known way to have SAS produce these CIs is to use publicly available SAS macros. The `%scoreci` macro is the only option if a stratified MN interval is required for an estimated RR or OR, and the same macro can also handle analysis of exposure-adjusted incidence rates, such as might be applied to adverse event data from clinical trials.

# Data used

The adcibc data stored [here](../data/adcibc.csv) was used in this example, creating a binary treatment variable `trt` taking the values of `Act` or `PBO` and a binary response variable `resp` taking the values of `Yes` or `No`. For this example, a response is defined as a score greater than 4, and the 3-level age group variable is used as a stratification variable.

``` sas
proc import datafile = 'data/adcibc.csv'
    out = adcibc
    dbms = csv
    replace;
    getnames = yes;
    guessingrows = max;
run;

data adcibc2 (keep=agegr1 trt resp) ;
    set adcibc;     
    if aval gt 4 then resp="Yes";
    else resp="No";     
    if trtp="Placebo" then trt="PBO";
    else trt="Act"; 
run;
 
* Sort to ensure that the outcome of interest ("Yes" in this example) is first;
* when using default COLUMN=1 option in the TABLES statement;
proc sort data=adcibc2; 
by agegr1 trt descending resp; 
run;  
```

# Online SAS macros

There are two available macros to use in SAS for the stratified MN method:

- [%scoreci](https://github.com/petelaud/ratesci-sas) - for stratified RD, RR and OR, with options for MH, INV or user-specified weighting.
- [%mn_cmh](https://pharmasug.org/proceedings/2025/SA/PharmaSUG-2025-SA-198.pdf) - stratified RD only, with MH weighting.

Both macros output the p-value for the CMH test for association along with the confidence interval. The `%scoreci` macro also produces a 1-sided hypothesis test against a user-specified null hypothesis value from the same score statistic (with or without skewness correction), for non-inferiority analysis (similar to the Farrington-Manning test for unstratified designs). `%scoreci` employs a more efficient root-finding procedure, so is able to generate results at greater precision with much faster computation times.

Note that both of these macros employ a simplified version of the Miettinen & Nurminen method, by replacing their proposed iterative weights with the simpler MH weights, as recommended by Lu[@lu2008].

# Code used

``` sas
*** First manipulate the data to a form for input to the %scoreci macro;
proc tabulate data=adcibc2 out=tab2;
 class agegr1 trt resp;
 table agegr1, (resp all), trt;
run;

data ds(keep = agegr1 e1 e0 n1 n0);
 set tab2;
 by _page_;
 retain e1 e0 n1 n0;
 * Initialise counts in case there are none in the observed data;
 if first._page_ then do;
  e1 = 0;
  e0 = 0;
  n1 = 0;
  n0 = 0;
 end;
 if upcase(trt) = "ACT" then do;
  if _type_ = "111" and resp = "Yes" then e1 = n;
  if _type_ = "110" then n1 = n;
 end;
 else if upcase(trt) = "PBO" then do;
  if _type_ = "111" and resp = "Yes" then e0 = n;
  if _type_ = "110" then n0 = n;
 end;
 if last._page_ then output;
run;

%SCORECI(DS = DS,
         CONTRAST = RD,
         SKEW = FALSE,
         LEVEL = 0.95,
         STRATIFY = TRUE,
         OUTPUT = TRUE,
         WEIGHT = 1);
```

*\[Output screenshot to be added\]*

There are occasional numerical differences between the results from the two macros. The PharmaSUG paper supporting the `%mn_cmh` macro claims they are based on "different methodological sources", but the underlying methodology appears to be identical. Discrepancies occur due to rare instances when `%mn_cmh` fails to calculate a stratum's contribution to the z-score. This happens for example when the observed proportions in a stratum are `3/8` and `5/8`. The following code produces a 95% CI of `(-0.324, 0.149)`, but if `x1` and `x2` are transposed the result is `(-0.190, 0.286)`. Hence the `%mn_cmh` macro cannot be relied upon to give consistent results.

``` sas
%strata(stratum=1, n1=8, n2=8, x1=3, x2=5);
%strata(stratum=2, n1=10, n2=10, x1=4, x2=4);
%strata(stratum=3, n1=10, n2=10, x1=4, x2=4);

%mn_cmh(critval=1.96);
```

The corresponding results from `%scoreci` are `(-0.324, 0.190)` and `(-0.190, 0.324)`.

```         
/******
NOTE: The dataset <input_dataset> contents need to be aggregated with 1 row per stratum of results.  With variables: N1, N0 for the sample size in the test and comparator groups and e1, e0 for the number of events in the test and comparator groups respectively
*******/
DATA DS1;
INPUT STRATUM E1 N1 E0 N0;
CARDS;
 1   3  8 5  8
 2   4 10 4 10
 3   4 10 4 10
;
run;
quit;

/******
NOTE that: 
skew = FALSE option, omits the skewness correction to give the Miettinen-Nurminen method. 
weight = 1 option uses MH weights
*******/
%SCORECI(DS = DS1,
         CONTRAST = RD,
         SKEW = FALSE,
         LEVEL = 0.95,
         STRATIFY = TRUE,
         OUTPUT = TRUE,
         WEIGHT = 1);
```

# SAS PROC FREQ on the SAS Viya platform

The stratified MN CI may be obtained in the SAS Viya platform, but only for the Risk Difference contrast.

``` sas
*** Specifying the stratified Miettinen-Nurminen (score) method in SAS Viya;
*** Input dataset structured as 1 row per subject (unless using a WEIGHT statement);
proc freq data = adcibc2; 
    tables  agegr1 * trt * resp / cmh commonriskdiff(CL=MN); 
run; 
```

`commonriskdiff(CL=MN)` applies the iterative weighting scheme as defined in the Miettinen-Nurminen 1985 paper. An alternative simpler Mantel-Haenszel weighting is often used instead, having been found to produce similar results in a 2008 ASA paper[@lu2008], and that version is obtained with `CL=MNMH`.

# Alternative methods in Base SAS v9.4 PROC FREQ

As mentioned, Base SAS (up to v9.4) does not produce a stratified MN confidence interval. You may think that a stratified MN confidence interval can be obtained using the following code. However, the `CL=MN` sub-option only implements the MN method for the per-stratum estimates, not the common RD estimate. See [SAS](https://support.sas.com/documentation/cdl/en/procstat/67528/HTML/default/viewer.htm#procstat_freq_details63.htm) for more detail of SAS's calculations.

``` sas
proc freq data = adcibc2;   
  tables agegr1 * trt * resp / cmh riskdiff(common CL=MN column=2) 
run;
```

As of SAS/STAT 15.4, `PROC FREQ` provides a `commonriskdiff(CL=xxx)` option giving a number of alternative methods for calculating CIs for common risk difference from stratified 2x2xK tables, including:

- Mantel-Haenszel with Sato variance estimate `(CL=MH)`

- Minimum Risk (Mehrotra and Railkar) method `(CL=MR)`

- The Summary Score (Agresti) method `(CL=score)`, starts with the per-stratum MN CLs, and combines their midpoints (rather than the point estimates), together with pseudo-variance estimates derived from the interval widths, to produce a pooled inverse-variance estimate of the common RD and its CI.

- Stratified Newcombe confidence intervals `(CL=newcombe)` using the method by Yan and Su (2010). These are constructed from stratified Wilson CIs for the common (overall) row proportions.

See [SAS Help](https://documentation.sas.com/doc/en/pgmsascdc/9.4_3.5/statug/statug_freq_details63.htm) for more details.

``` sas
proc freq data = adcibc (where=(trtpn ne 54 and agegr1 ne ">80")); 
    tables  agegr1 * trtp *  sex / cmh commonriskdiff(CL=SCORE TEST=SCORE); 
run; 
```

    tables  agegr1 * trtp *  sex / cmh commonriskdiff(CL= newcombe); 
run;
